title: Temperature Control — Cook, Chill, Hold
blurb: How temperature stops bacteria multiplying: cooking, chilling, hot-holding, cooling cooked food and recording it all.
siteNotes: Which probe thermometers are used and how they are calibrated and cleaned
Where temperature records are kept and who checks them
The venue's cooling method and where cooked food is chilled
Who you report a warm fridge or undercooked food to
legalNotes: Chilled food at 8°C or below and hot-held food at 63°C or above: Food Temperature Control regulations in England (Food Safety (Temperature Control) Regulations 1995, as amended). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1995/2200
Food safety management based on HACCP principles and records: Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, art. 5, as retained in law in England. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2004/852
CHECK: the trainer gives the danger zone as roughly 8°C to 63°C. FSA guidance describes it as roughly 5°C to 63°C. The 8°C figure is the legal maximum for chilled food. Kept as the trainer says.

CHECK: the trainer gives 75°C as a "common target" core temperature. FSA guidance describes 70°C for 2 minutes (or equivalent) as the standard; 75°C is a common venue target. Confirm the venue figure.
CHECK: cooling "ideally within about 90 minutes" is industry guidance rather than a legal figure; confirm it matches the venue procedure.
CHECK: hot food held at 63°C or above has limited legal exceptions (for example, short service periods); none are taught here.

cards.title: Temperature Control — Cook, Chill, Hold
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- name the danger zone and why it matters
- cook, chill and hold food at the right temperatures
- record temperatures and report problems

cards.title: Temperature controls bacteria
cards.body: Temperature is one of the most powerful weapons against food poisoning, because it controls whether harmful bacteria multiply or are killed. The zone to fear is the "danger zone", roughly 8°C to 63°C, where bacteria multiply happily.

cards.title: Hot all the way through
cards.body: Get food properly hot all the way through. A core temperature of 75°C is a common target that kills the bacteria that make people ill.

cards.title: Keep cold food cold, hot food hot
cards.body: The rules are simple. Keep chilled food cold and hot food hot.

items.title: Chilled
items.text: 8°C or below by law. We aim for 5°C or below.

items.title: In between
items.text: The danger zone. Keep food out of it.

cards.title: Cool quickly, then fridge
cards.body: If you are cooling cooked food to store it, cool it quickly (ideally within about 90 minutes) and get it into the fridge. Do not leave it sitting out in the danger zone.

right.title: Do not
items: Let it stay in the danger zone

cards.title: Write it down
cards.body:
Do not just check, record. Checking and writing down temperatures for cooking, chilling and hot-holding is part of our food safety system and proves we are keeping food safe.

> If a fridge is running warm or food is not reaching the right temperature, report it straight away.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Danger zone is roughly 8°C to 63°C: get through it fast
- Cook to a core temperature of 75°C, checked with a clean, calibrated probe
- Chilled 8°C or below by law, aim for 5°C; hot 63°C or above
- Cool cooked food quickly, ideally within about 90 minutes
- Record temperatures and report problems straight away

cards.why: It is roughly 8°C to 63°C, where bacteria multiply happily.

cards.q: A common core cooking temperature target is 75°C.
cards.why: A core temperature of 75°C kills the bacteria that make people ill.

cards.q: Hot food should be held at…
options: Any temperature if it is covered
cards.why: Hot food should be kept at 63°C or above so it stays out of the danger zone.

cards.q: Chilled food should be kept at 8°C or below by law.
cards.why: 8°C or below is the legal limit, and we aim for 5°C or below.

cards.q: How should you check a food's core temperature?
options: By its colour once it is cooked
By pressing it with your finger
With a clean, calibrated probe in the thickest part
By feeling that the outside is hot
cards.why: Use a probe in the thickest part rather than guessing by colour.

cards.q: Cooked food you're storing should be cooled quickly, not left sitting out.
cards.why: Cool it quickly, ideally within about 90 minutes, and get it into the fridge.

cards.q: Why do bacteria love the danger zone?
cards.why: The danger zone is where harmful bacteria multiply happily.

cards.q: Temperatures should be recorded, not just checked.
cards.why: Written records are part of our food safety system and prove food is safe.

cards.q: What should you do if a fridge is running warm?
options: Turn it up and carry on
Wait until the end of service
Report it straight away and check the food
Move the food to the top shelf
cards.why: Report it straight away so it can be sorted before anyone is put at risk.
Clean and sanitise the probe between uses.
